title.rendered: Love Your Enemies: The Gospel For Today

excerpt.rendered: The traditional teaching of Jesus’ day was tidy. Love your neighbor. Hate your enemy. It felt fair. It felt achievable. Jesus tore it in half.

content.rendered:
The traditional teaching of Jesus’ day was tidy. Love your neighbor. Hate your enemy. It felt fair. It felt achievable. Jesus tore it in half.

The Gospel For Today | Wednesday, September 23, 2026

Today’s Scripture

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you, that you may be sons of your Father in heaven.”
Matthew 5:43-45 (NKJV)

Today’s Message

The traditional teaching of Jesus’ day was tidy. Love your neighbour. Hate your enemy. It matched what came naturally to the human heart. It felt fair. It felt achievable. It let the listener draw a clean line between the ones deserving kindness and the ones deserving retaliation. Some of the most influential rabbinical schools of the day taught it. The Dead Sea Scrolls of the Qumran community taught it explicitly, that the sons of light were commanded to hate the sons of darkness. So when Jesus stood on the hillside in Galilee and said, “You have heard that it was said,” He was not inventing a straw man. He was quoting the teaching every listener had grown up with. And then, with the four words that reordered the moral universe of the ancient world, He tore it in half. “But I say to you.”

“But I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you, that you may be sons of your Father in heaven.” Four commands, each aimed at a different level of hostility. Love the enemy. Bless the one cursing you. Do good to the one hating you. Pray for the one persecuting you. Each command escalates. Each one costs more than the last. Together they define a way of life that has no precedent in the ancient world, and no natural home in the human heart.

The Passion Translation captures the radical nature of what Jesus is asking: “However, I say to you, love your enemy, bless the one who curses you, do something wonderful for the one who hates you, and respond to the very ones who persecute you by praying for them. For that will reveal your identity as children of your heavenly Father” (Matthew 5:44-45 TPT). The Amplified Bible Classic Edition adds: “But I tell you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, To show that you are the children of your Father Who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:44-45 AMPC). Notice the outcome Jesus attaches to enemy-love. Not that it will change the enemy, though sometimes it does. Not that it will make life easier for the believer, because it will not. The outcome is identity. Enemy-love reveals whose children we are. Sons and daughters of a Father who Himself sends rain on the just and the unjust.

This is one of the hardest commandments Jesus ever spoke. It is also the most unmistakably distinctive mark of Kingdom life. Everyone loves their friends. Even the most secular household loves its own. What separates the disciple of Jesus from the wider world is what they do with the person who has hurt them, cursed them, hated them, or persecuted them. In the natural order of things, hostility begets hostility. Curse begets curse. Wrong begets wrong. Jesus taught His disciples to interrupt that cycle by refusing to return it in kind. Love. Bless. Do good. Pray. Every one of these verbs is a way of returning good for evil, and every one of them draws on the finished work of the cross, where Jesus Himself demonstrated exactly what enemy-love looks like when it goes all the way.

For Gospelbuzz readers today, this closes our four-day walk through the great commandments of Jesus. Love God. Love neighbour. Love one another. Love enemies. The four commands form the arc of Kingdom life. Wherever you are reading this from, in Lagos or London or Manila or Nairobi or Sao Paulo, there is likely a name on your heart today of someone who has wronged you. A name that has been sitting in your mind, unforgiven, unblessed, unprayed for. Bring that name to Jesus today. Ask Him for the grace to love, bless, do good, and pray, not because the person deserves it, but because the Father has already treated you the same way in Christ. Enemy-love is not a technique. It is the outflow of a heart that has itself been loved when it was still an enemy. Walk in that today.

Prayer

Father, I acknowledge that You loved me while I was still Your enemy. Christ died for me before I ever turned toward You. Today I bring the name that has been sitting in my heart, the person who has hurt me, cursed me, hated me, or wronged me. In the strength of the love You first poured out on me, I choose to love them today. I choose to bless them. I choose to do good to them. I choose to pray for them. I refuse to return curse for curse. I refuse to feed the cycle of hostility. I show whose child I am by loving as my Father in heaven loves. In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Declaration

I love my enemies as my Father in heaven loved me when I was His enemy. I bless. I do good. I pray. I refuse the cycle of hostility. My love reveals whose child I am.
